## Physical intelligence and its substrate

Physical intelligence is the ability of a learning system to model a physical system and to act on it. A material during processing, a water network under pumping, and a power plant following its load are governed by ordinary or partial differential equations with initial conditions, boundary conditions, and external forcing. To model such a system is to solve those equations for the conditions at hand. To act on it is to compute a decision from the solution. My work covers both steps and the error that passes between them, in three directions.

## A. Physical systems in science and engineering

**Science.** With [Professor Fengqi You](https://www.peese.org/professor/) at Cornell, the system is a materials processing step. Its state is a temperature and composition field, and the decision is a process set-point or a trajectory of settings.

**Engineering.** From my Ph.D. with [Professor Jingcheng Wang](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37280547200) at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, the systems are urban water supply coupled to the electricity market, and hot-strip rolling. Their states are water demand, network pressure, day-ahead electricity price, and rolling energy. The decisions are pump schedules, energy purchases, and controller actions.

Each system supplies its governing dynamics to direction B and its decision to direction C.

## B. Solving the dynamics with neural networks

The solution operator of a physical system maps initial conditions, boundary conditions, geometry, and forcing to the solution field over space and time. A neural operator approximates that map, so a trained model returns the field for new conditions in one forward pass instead of a new simulation. I study three properties of such a model. Its autoregressive rollout has to stay accurate over the horizon a controller needs. Its sensitivities to boundary inputs and process settings have to be accurate enough for an optimizer. Physics-constrained training and hybrid schemes that keep part of the numerical solver have to reduce the training data it needs. A model with these properties solves the dynamics. A model that only reproduces one simulation is a surrogate.

In the engineering systems this direction began with learned temporal dynamics. [Lag-free demand forecasting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2024.124508) corrects the delayed response of a learned model near a demand turning point. [Uncertain pressure regression](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSS.2023.3272330) separates the pressure response to measured inputs from the residual variation caused by unmeasured disturbances. A [series-concatenation model](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASE.2023.3299185) of hot-strip rolling passes the state of each rolling pass to the next, so the multi-step error stops accumulating.

## C. The model-to-decision gap

A learned model is wrong by a small amount everywhere. Once a controller or an optimizer decides with it, the quantity that matters is the change in the decision, not the error in the field. I call the difference between the decision computed from the learned model and the decision computed from the true dynamics the **model-to-decision gap**. Over most of the state space the gap is proportional to the model error. Near a critical point, a bifurcation, a regime boundary, or an active constraint, the decision changes qualitatively with the state, and the same model error moves an operating point across a fold or a schedule across a capacity limit. I measure the gap as regret, closed-loop cost, and constraint violation, locate the regions where it is large, and use it as the training signal for the solver.

[Stochastic Predict-Then-Optimize](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSG.2025.3601238) trains a probabilistic electricity-cost forecast through the water-supply schedule it induces. A differentiable upper bound on the optimality gap carries the change in scheduling cost back to the forecast. A [reinforcement learning controller for constrained nonlinear systems](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.2023.3344883) keeps state and input constraints active during learning through a control barrier function. [Adaptive optimal control with multiple time-scale eligibility traces](https://doi.org/10.1109/CDC49753.2023.10383316) follows the credit for a decision over several horizons. [DRIFT](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2026.133261) asks the same question of a generated trajectory and tests whether the output of a diffusion model respects the LiDAR geometry it moves through.

## Research map

| Direction | Question | Evaluated by |
|---|---|---|
| A. Physical systems in science and engineering | What are the state, the dynamics, and the decision of each system? | The system's own operating cost, feasibility, and constraints |
| B. Solving the dynamics with neural networks | Does the learned operator return the solution field for new conditions, fast enough for design and control? | Field error, rollout error, and sensitivity error |
| C. The model-to-decision gap | Where in the state space does the model error change the decision, and by how much? | Regret, closed-loop cost, and constraint violation |

[Publications](/publications/) and [research projects](/projects/) are grouped by these directions.
